---
title: "Costing a study"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")
```

```{r setup}
library(MMSpower)
```

A design that meets its statistical target is only useful if it can be paid
for. `estimate_cost()` puts a price on a design, and because it takes its
inputs straight from the design functions, it can be used to compare
designs that are statistically equivalent but cost very different amounts.

All costs in this article are **illustrative**, in an unnamed currency
unit. Replace them with figures from your own budget.

## The cost model

`estimate_cost()` splits a study's cost into two parts.

**Stage costs.** A sample passes through up to three stages, each with its
own cost per person or sample:

- **screened** (`n_screened`, `cost_per_screened`): everyone screened at
  enrolment, covering consent, interview and a rapid test or microscopy;
- **collected** (`n_collected`, `cost_per_collected`): everyone a sample is
  collected from, covering a dried blood spot or blood draw, storage and
  shipping;
- **sequenced** (`n_sequenced`, `cost_per_sequenced`): every sample taken
  through the molecular laboratory, covering extraction, PCR or sequencing
  and data management.

The stages are nested, not added on top of each other. `n_collected` is a
subset of `n_screened`: for example, only those who test positive at
screening have a sample collected. `n_sequenced` is a subset of
`n_collected`: what is left after lost or failed samples. A person is
counted at every stage they reach, so `n_screened` is at least
`n_collected`, which is at least `n_sequenced`, and the function stops with
an error otherwise. Each stage's cost is the cost of that stage alone, not
of everything up to it.

**Site costs.** Each site has a fixed cost (training, equipment,
administration) and a transport cost.

Give only the stages a study has. The design functions return the number of
samples needed at analysis, so their `n` is `n_sequenced`. With a single
all-in cost per sample, that one stage is enough:

```{r}
estimate_cost(n_sequenced = 400, cost_per_sequenced = 40)
```

`stage_cost` gives the cost of each stage, and adds up to `variable_cost`.
With sites, give the number of sites and the cost per site:

```{r}
estimate_cost(n_sequenced = 400, cost_per_sequenced = 40, n_sites = 20,
              fixed_cost_per_site = 2000, transport_cost_per_site = 600)
```

Site costs need not be the same everywhere. Remote sites usually cost more
to reach, so either per-site cost can be given as one value per site.
Adding a `budget` reports how much would be left over (negative if the
study is over budget):

```{r}
transport <- c(200, 200, 300, 400, 600, 800, 1200, 1500)
estimate_cost(n_sequenced = 240, cost_per_sequenced = 40, n_sites = 8,
              fixed_cost_per_site = 2000, transport_cost_per_site = transport,
              budget = 35000)
```

## Costing the people actually enrolled

A design's `n` is only the last stage. To reach it, a study has to collect
samples from more people, to allow for losses, and screen more people
still, if only those who test positive go on to have a sample collected.
"Allowing for dropout and suspected cases" in the
[Estimating prevalence](tutorial-prevalence.html) tutorial works out these
numbers; here we cost them.

That tutorial's design has 20 people per site, with an ICC of 0.05:

```{r}
d_prev <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
c(n_sites = d_prev$n_sites, n = d_prev$n)
```

Work back from the analysis one stage at a time, per site so that every
site delivers its share. With 10% of samples expected to be lost, divide by
0.9 to get the number collected; with 40% of those screened expected to
test positive, divide again by 0.4 to get the number screened:

```{r}
per_site_sequenced <- d_prev$n_per_site
per_site_collected <- ceiling(per_site_sequenced / 0.9)
per_site_screened  <- ceiling(per_site_collected / 0.4)

n_sequenced <- d_prev$n
n_collected <- d_prev$n_sites * per_site_collected
n_screened  <- d_prev$n_sites * per_site_screened
c(screened = n_screened, collected = n_collected, sequenced = n_sequenced)
```

Then cost all three stages, here 3 per person screened, 10 per sample
collected and 40 per sample sequenced:

```{r}
staged <- estimate_cost(n_screened  = n_screened,  cost_per_screened  = 3,
                        n_collected = n_collected, cost_per_collected = 10,
                        n_sequenced = n_sequenced, cost_per_sequenced = 40,
                        n_sites = d_prev$n_sites, fixed_cost_per_site = 2000,
                        transport_cost_per_site = 600)
staged$stage_cost
staged$total_cost
```

Screening `r format(n_screened, big.mark = ",")` people and collecting
`r n_collected` samples add
`r format(sum(staged$stage_cost[c("screened", "collected")]), big.mark = ",")`
to the `r format(staged$stage_cost[["sequenced"]], big.mark = ",")` spent on
sequencing. Costing only the `r n_sequenced` samples at analysis would have
missed both stages.

If samples are expected to fail in the laboratory rather than be lost
before it, the failed ones are still paid for: cost `n_sequenced` as the
number of samples sent to the laboratory, here `n_collected`, rather than
the number expected to succeed.

## Comparing designs

The main use of `estimate_cost()` is choosing between designs. Suppose we
want to estimate a prevalence of around 30% to within ±5 percentage points,
with an ICC of 0.05. `design_precision()` can meet that target with many
combinations of sites and people per site. Few people per site needs many
sites; many people per site needs fewer sites, but a larger design effect
means more people in total.

Work out the design for each number of people per site from 5 to 60, and
cost each one:

```{r}
cost_per_sample <- 40     # all-in cost per sample sequenced
site_cost       <- 2000   # fixed cost per site
transport_cost  <- 600    # transport cost per site

per_site <- 5:60
designs <- do.call(rbind, lapply(per_site, function(s) {
  des  <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.3, moe = 0.05, n_per_site = s, icc = 0.05)
  cost <- estimate_cost(n_sequenced = des$n, cost_per_sequenced = cost_per_sample,
                        n_sites = des$n_sites,
                        fixed_cost_per_site = site_cost,
                        transport_cost_per_site = transport_cost)
  data.frame(n_per_site = s, n_sites = des$n_sites, n = des$n,
             deff = des$deff, total_cost = cost$total_cost)
}))
head(designs)
```

```{r}
best <- designs[which.min(designs$total_cost), ]
best
```

```{r, warning = FALSE, fig.alt = "Total study cost against people per site, falling steeply then levelling off, with the cheapest design marked."}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(designs, aes(x = n_per_site, y = total_cost / 1000)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#1B2A41", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(colour = "#1B2A41", size = 1.2) +
  geom_point(data = best, colour = "#C0392B", size = 4) +
  geom_text(data = best, aes(label = sprintf("%d sites of %d", n_sites, n_per_site)),
            colour = "#6B7280", vjust = -1.4) +
  labs(x = "People per site", y = "Total cost (thousands)") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 13)
```

Every point on this curve gives the same precision. On the left, sampling 5
people per site needs `r designs$n_sites[1]` sites, and the site costs
dominate. Moving right, each extra person per site saves sites, and the
cost falls quickly. Past a point the saving stops: the design effect keeps
growing, so the extra people needed to make up for it cost more than the
sites they save. The cheapest design here is `r best$n_sites` sites of
`r best$n_per_site` people (`r best$n` in all, design effect
`r best$deff`), costing `r format(best$total_cost, big.mark = ",")`.

The curve is jagged because the number of sites is a whole number: a design
that needs 23.1 sites pays for 24. Near the bottom the curve is also quite
flat, so designs a little either side of the cheapest cost much the same.
That leaves room to choose on practical grounds, such as how many people a
field team can sample at a site in a day.

The shape depends on the ratio of site cost to sample cost. When sites are
expensive relative to samples, the cheapest design has more people per
site; when samples are expensive (for example, with whole-genome
sequencing), it has fewer. A higher ICC also pushes towards fewer people
per site, since each additional person at a site is worth less.

## Costing a comparison of two groups

The same works for any design function. For `design_difference()`, note
that `n` is already the total across both groups, but `n_sites` is given
per group, so the number of sites to cost is `sum(n_sites)`:

```{r}
dd <- design_difference(prevalence1 = 0.10, prevalence2 = 0.20,
                        n_per_site1 = 20, icc = 0.05)
dd$n
dd$n_sites
estimate_cost(n_sequenced = dd$n, cost_per_sequenced = cost_per_sample,
              n_sites = sum(dd$n_sites),
              fixed_cost_per_site = site_cost,
              transport_cost_per_site = transport_cost)
```

If the two regions have different costs (one is much further away, say),
call `estimate_cost()` once per region and add the totals.

## Fitting a budget

To find which designs fit a fixed budget, keep the rows of the table above
that come in under it. With a budget of 110,000:

```{r}
budget <- 110000
fits <- designs[designs$total_cost <= budget, ]
range(fits$n_per_site)
```

`r nrow(fits)` of the `r nrow(designs)` designs meet the precision target
within budget, with between `r min(fits$n_per_site)` and
`r max(fits$n_per_site)` people per site. Because the curve is jagged, not
every value in that range fits; check the table rather than assuming it
does. If no row fits, the target itself has to change: a wider margin of
error, or a cheaper laboratory method. For the chosen design, `budget`
shows what is left for contingencies:

```{r}
estimate_cost(n_sequenced = best$n, cost_per_sequenced = cost_per_sample,
              n_sites = best$n_sites,
              fixed_cost_per_site = site_cost,
              transport_cost_per_site = transport_cost,
              budget = budget)$budget_remaining
```
